# Forensic Dossier — Koninklijke Ahold Delhaize N.V. (AD.AS)
*Interrogator / Investment Committee — capital-at-risk read. Transcripts: FY24 (2025-02-12), Q1'25 (2025-05-07), Q2'25 (2025-08-06), Q3'25 (2025-11-05), FY25 (2026-02-11). Financials: screener scan + TTM to 2026-03-31.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story across these five calls is strikingly *stationary* — by design. Management anchors every call to one unchanging frame: the **"Growing Together"** strategy unveiled May/June 2024 (a 4-year plan promising ~4% sales CAGR and an *average* ~4% underlying operating margin). The FY24 call (2025-02-12) opens with Muller's three words — "commitment, consistency and clarity" — and the subsequent four calls are essentially serial proof-points against that scorecard. There is no thesis shift, no pivot, no quietly-dropped growth driver. That consistency is itself the most important narrative datum: this is a management team that says the same thing for five straight quarters and then largely delivers it.

What *does* evolve is the **emphasis within the frame**:
- **US repositioning intensity ramps then normalizes.** FY24/Q1'25 are dominated by Stop & Shop surgery — store closures (32 underperformers closed by Q2'25), the $1bn/4-yr US price-investment program, "40% of stores" repriced (Q1'25) climbing to ">65% of the fleet" by FY25. By FY25 the language softens from "decisive and deliberate actions" to "steadily improving trends in comparable sales growth, including volume growth."
- **Omnichannel profitability becomes the new hero metric.** Q2'25 introduces the milestone — "on a fully allocated basis, we have reached e-commerce profitability for the total company" — and it recurs every call after. This is a genuine narrative *expansion*: online shifts from margin-dilutive admission (FY24: online growth "is, of course, dilutive to our overall margin") to a structural growth/margin tailwind (FY25: "online is a core driver of that growth").
- **AI / retail-media is layered on as the 2026 forward driver.** Largely absent from FY24 substance, by FY25 it is a featured block (new CTO Jan Brecht, "EUR 2.7 billion in annual CapEx" with a "growing share" to tech/AI, retail media "an increasingly important growth machine").
- **M&A bolt-ons accrete quietly:** Profi (Romania, +€3bn sales, closed Q1'25), Louis Delhaize (Belgium, +303 stores, FY25). These densify rather than transform.

Net: a stable, executing defensive compounder telling a low-drama compounding story — not a turnaround, not a melt-up.

Ahold Delhaize is a pan-Atlantic grocery operator — it runs Albert Heijn and bol in the Netherlands, Delhaize in Belgium, Stop & Shop, Food Lion, Hannaford and Giant in the eastern United States, and Profi/Mega Image in Romania. It is a low-margin, high-volume, capital-intensive food retailer. The investment question is narrow: at roughly four times free cash flow, is the market pricing a structurally shrinking business, or is it simply ignoring a steady, cash-generative compounder?

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story has been remarkably consistent — almost monotonous — across all eight quarters, which for a defensive grocer is itself a positive signal. The spine is management's "Growing Together" strategy, unveiled in mid-2024 and repeated nearly verbatim every quarter since: grow sales faster than the industry at roughly a 4% compound annual rate, hold a leading underlying operating margin of about 4%, and convert that into steady earnings and free-cash-flow growth that funds dividends and buybacks.

What evolved within that frame is the emphasis. Early in 2025 the focus was on the heavy lifting — the Stop & Shop turnaround in the US (store closures, a $1 billion four-year price-investment program), the Belgium "Future Plan" franchise conversion, and integrating the Profi acquisition in Romania. By late 2025 and into the February 2026 call, the tone shifted toward harvesting: e-commerce reached full profitability "on a fully allocated basis" (a milestone management flagged as arriving earlier than expected), own-brand penetration climbed toward 39.8% group-wide (close to 50% in Europe), and retail media (advertising income) was repeatedly upgraded to a "growth machine."

Two growth drivers were introduced and amplified over time: retail media / advertising income, and artificial-intelligence-driven productivity (forecasting, store-first fulfillment, the Albert Heijn app, bol's "Spot & Shop"). Nothing material was quietly dropped — the Stop & Shop turnaround is still openly a multi-year project ("done in year four"), which is honest rather than evasive.

| Management claim | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "~4% sales CAGR" (Growing Together) | Revenue €86.98B (2022) → €92.35B (2025); 3-yr CAGR +2.0%, latest year +3.4%; FY2025 net sales +5.9% (Profi/M&A-aided) | **Partly supported.** Organic comparable growth (~3.2% ex-gas in 2025) is real but the headline 4% leans on acquisitions and currency. |
| "~4% underlying operating margin, leading" | Reported underlying margin 4.0% in 2025; screener net margin 2.4%, gross 26.5% (stable) | **Supported.** The 4% is an *underlying operating* margin (pre-unusuals); the thin 2.4% net margin is normal for grocery and consistent. |
| "Strong free cash flow funding returns" | TTM free cash flow €5.27B; FY2025 FCF strong; 2026 guide ≥€2.3B; P/FCF ~4.2x | **Strongly supported** — and the crux of the value case. | "Online now profitable, fully allocated" | Margin stable, no separate disclosure | **Plausible but unverifiable from the financials** — management stopped breaking it out, which removes the ability to check it independently. |
| Stop & Shop "improving trends, gaining share" | US impairments ran ~€200M+/yr; management insists this is "incidental," not a run-rate | **Watch item.** The repeated US store impairments are the one place the narrative is richer than the evidence. |

The headline takeaway: the financials *corroborate* the cash-generation and margin claims, which are the load-bearing planks of a deep-value thesis. The growth claims are real but modest and partly bought. Returns are pedestrian — return on equity 14.6%, return on invested capital 7.3% — acceptable for capital-intensive grocery but not evidence of a widening moat.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Stable-to-rising, with disciplined restraint.** Management's confidence is steady and, if anything, firmer by the February 2026 call. Frans Muller (CEO) repeatedly bats away requests for segment-level or quarterly margin guidance — "live with the group guidance on margin, Rob" (May 2025) — which reads as discipline, not evasion, because the *group* guidance is specific and gets reiterated. The language stays offensive (growth, investment, densify-and-grow) rather than retreating into pure cost-defense, even while acknowledging a "volatile" macro backdrop (tariffs, egg prices, SNAP-benefit delays, Serbian price controls, Romanian VAT). CFO Jolanda Poots-Bijl is consistently the more conservative voice ("we take out pain rather early than later" on impairments), which lends credibility.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High.** The screener shows an earnings-beat rate of 6 of the last 7 quarters (86%). Across the transcript window management set group targets (≈4% growth, ≈4% margin, free cash flow floors) and then delivered against them — FY2025 landed at 4.0% underlying margin, +7.8% underlying EPS, and a reaffirmed dividend (+6% to €1.24) and €1 billion buyback. The Q1 2026 update reiterated full-year guidance (free cash flow of at least €2.3 billion, ~4% margin, mid-to-high-single-digit EPS growth) despite a seasonally negative Q1 free-cash-flow figure that management correctly pre-flagged as timing. There is a mild sandbagging pattern (the conservative €2.3B floor against ~€5.3B trailing). Reliability: **High.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts pushed hardest on three things, and management's handling tells you where the soft spots are:
- **US margin trajectory and Stop & Shop** — the most-asked topic, and the one management most consistently refuses to quantify quarter-by-quarter. The price-investment program ($1B over four years) is a margin headwind they ask the market to take on faith.
- **US store impairments** (UBS, August 2025) — a "EUR 200 million plus per year run rate" that management firmly disputes as incidental (Stop & Shop closures, Fresh Direct, fulfillment-center exits). If impairments persist beyond those one-offs, it would undercut the "store-first model is working" claim.
- **Profi (Romania)** — analysts flagged cut full-year sales guidance for Profi (November 2025), which management attributed to Romanian VAT and food-voucher timing, not structural weakness.

None of these has yet "turned into bad news," but the US price-investment margin drag is the live tension.

🟢 Reaffirmed and growing capital returns — €1B buyback plus a 40–50% payout dividend (+6% in 2025).
🟢 E-commerce reaching full-allocated profitability earlier than planned (February 2026) — removes a long-standing margin drag.
🟢 Consistent guidance delivery (86% beat rate) and a strong Piotroski financial-health score of 8/9.
🟢 Retail-media / advertising income emerging as a genuine high-margin growth lever.
🔴 Recurring US store impairments (~€200M/yr) that management insists are one-offs — needs to actually fade.
🔴 Online profitability de-disclosed ("we look at it holistically now") — convenient timing removes a check.
🔴 Returns are merely adequate (return on invested capital 7.3%) and the $1B US price-investment program is a self-imposed multi-year margin drag.
🟡 Growth is acquisition-assisted (Profi, Louis Delhaize), so organic momentum is slower than the headline.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The vocabulary migrated from "turnaround" language (Stop & Shop "interventions," Belgium "Future Plan") toward "scale and harvest" language (retail media "growth machine," "build once, scale across brands," AI productivity). New executive voices — a new Chief Technology Officer (Jan Brecht) and a US Chief Commercial and Digital Officer (Keith) — signal a deliberate tilt toward technology-and-data monetization rather than store operations. Management's framing of bol versus Chinese marketplaces (Temu/SHEIN) leaning on "European regulation on quality" is a subtle moat-defense argument for the Dutch e-commerce asset. Capital allocation is unflashy and consistent: organic capex (~€2.7B/yr), bolt-on M&A in adjacent geographies, and a steady buyback-plus-dividend — no leverage adventures, no transformational deal.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** This is a well-run, predictable, cash-generative defensive grocer executing a credible plan and returning cash steadily. It is neither strengthening dramatically nor deteriorating.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** there is no discrete catalyst here. The capital-return program is real but *ongoing and self-renewing* — a €1 billion buyback already roughly a third executed and a 40–50% payout dividend — not a one-time event that forces a re-rating. The thesis is "buy a stable cash machine at four times free cash flow and collect the yield while the discount slowly closes," which depends on patience, not an event.

**Moat:** narrow but real — regional scale economics and density (number-one or number-two in ~80% of its US trade areas; ~50% own-brand penetration in Europe) plus the Dutch e-commerce franchise (bol). It is a scale-cost and local-density moat, not a switching-cost one. The evidence says **stable**, not widening: return on invested capital at 7.3% is steady but not rising, and gross margin is flat at 26.5%.

**Secular threat: manageable.** Grocery is the most defensible corner of retail against e-commerce channel-shift — perishables, local fulfillment, and thin margins protect the incumbent, and Ahold is itself the online share-gainer (online +12.9% in 2025) rather than the victim. This is not a melting terminal-value situation; the cheapness is a fear-print on a low-growth, low-margin business, not a value trap.

on has yet turned into a negative surprise.

long-standing structural drag.

almost defensive framing of impairments as "conservative, store-by-store, take the pain early"

consistency read.

having just reached online profitability — so the threat is **manageable**, not terminal. The
cheapness is best read as a modest fair-print on a steady compounder, not a structurally shrinking
base and not a deep bargain.

# Ahold Delhaize (AD.AS) — A Deep Dive on Management and the Setup

Ahold Delhaize is a large, mature food retailer with roughly €92 billion in annual
sales, split across the United States (Stop & Shop, Giant, Food Lion, Hannaford) and
Europe (Albert Heijn in the Netherlands, Delhaize in Belgium, plus Central and
Southeastern Europe and the online marketplace bol). The transcripts run from the
2024 full-year call (February 2025) through the third-quarter 2025 call (November 2025).
The through-line is a company executing a defined four-year plan called "Growing
Together," and doing so with unusual consistency. This dossier tests that story against
the hard numbers.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story barely shifts across the four calls — and for a defensive grocer, that steadiness
is itself the message. In February 2025, chief executive Frans Muller framed the year in
three words: "commitment, consistency and clarity," and set out the plan's headline math —
grow sales at a roughly 4% compound annual rate, hold an underlying operating margin of
around 4%, and deliver sustainable earnings growth over the 2025–2028 window. Every
subsequent call restates the same targets almost verbatim. By the third quarter of 2025,
Muller was still leading with the same "Growing Together" framing and the same $1 billion
US price-investment commitment.

What evolves is not the destination but the proof points. Early calls emphasized fixing
troubled assets — closing underperforming Stop & Shop stores, completing the Belgium
"Future Plan" store-franchising transition, and integrating the newly acquired Romanian
chain Profi (over €3 billion of added sales). By mid-2025 the emphasis rotated to
offense: reaching company-wide online profitability "on a fully allocated basis" (a
milestone management called out proudly in the second quarter of 2025), double-digit online
grocery growth for a fifth straight quarter, and own-brand penetration climbing toward a
45% ambition. No growth driver was quietly dropped; the plan is remarkably intact.

narrative runs slightly ahead of the trajectory is the "sustainable earnings growth" phrase —
the five-year EPS path (€2.17 in 2021 to €2.50 in 2025) is a compound rate under 4%, with a
visible 2023–2024 dip driven by US margin pressure and impairments. This is a low-single-digit
grower dressed, fairly but generously, as a compounder.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

firms as online profitability arrives. In February 2025 Muller was already refusing to be
pinned to segment guidance ("you ask us for almost weekly guidances"). By August 2025 the
tone was celebratory on the e-commerce profitability milestone — "we celebrate this here
in-house because it's a very conservative look at fully allocated. It comes earlier than we
expected." The language stays offensive (growth, volume, market-share gains) rather than
defensive, even while acknowledging a genuinely hard macro backdrop: US SNAP-benefit delays,
Romanian VAT increases, egg-price spikes, tariffs. The chief financial officer, Jolanda
Poots-Bijl, is consistently precise and unflappable on cash-flow and impairment questions.

**High.** The screener records a beat on 6 of the last 7 quarters (86%). Guidance given in
early 2025 — around 4% margin, mid-to-high-single-digit EPS growth, free cash flow of at least
€2.2–2.3 billion — was reiterated intact through Q1 2026 despite a negative first-quarter free
cash flow number that management correctly pre-framed as working-capital phasing, not
deterioration. There is a mild sandbagging pattern: they guide conservatively (the "around 4%"
margin has a flexibility buffer built in, by their own admission) and then deliver at or above.
For a defensive holding, this is exactly the reliability profile you want.

The recurring analyst worry is **US margin trajectory** — specifically whether the $1 billion
Stop & Shop-led price investment permanently compresses US profitability. Management
repeatedly declines to give regional margin guidance ("we don't give guidance on a regional
level"), which is the single most-deflected topic across all four calls. A second pressure
point was the **step-up in US store impairments** (a UBS analyst flagged a ~€200 million-plus
annual run-rate); management pushed back hard, attributing it to one-off Stop & Shop and
Fresh Direct closures rather than a structural NPV reassessment. That pushback is plausible but
worth watching — impairments are where grocery trouble surfaces first. Nothing analysts pressed
on has yet turned into a negative surprise.

🟢 Company-wide online profitability reached on a fully-allocated basis (Q2 2025) — removes a
long-standing structural drag.
🟢 Consistent buyback plus dividend; €1 billion repurchase roughly 40% executed by mid-2026.
🟢 Number-one or number-two market positions in ~80% of US markets served; genuine local scale.
🟢 European own-brand share already ~50%, a real margin and loyalty lever.

pharmacy mix are dilutive.
🔴 The five-year EPS record is essentially flat compounded; "growth" is aspiration more than track.
🔴 Rising US store impairments, even if explained, sit on the watch-list.

metric (price-to-free-cash-flow), not across the board.

marketplace, and of **retail media** (advertising sold against shopper data) as
"complementary income streams." Management is steering the narrative toward higher-margin,
capital-light income to offset thin core grocery economics. A second signal: the repeated,
almost defensive framing of impairments as "conservative, store-by-store, take the pain early"
— a company that impairs early is either genuinely prudent or managing a slow US structural
issue. The evidence so far favors prudent. There were no disruptive management changes; the
same chief executive and chief financial officer carry all four calls, which supports the
consistency read.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**STABLE.** This is a well-run, disciplined defensive grocer that does what it says, returns
cash, and has removed its biggest structural drag (online losses). The single most important
thing the director must weigh before sizing: **this is a quality-and-consistency story, not a
mispricing story.** The stock trades near or slightly above conservative intrinsic value, the
€1 billion buyback is being executed at prices at or above today's, and the peer group (Carrefour
around 11x forward earnings, Kroger around 12x) is not cheaper than Ahold Delhaize's roughly 13x.
The apparent bargain lives entirely in the price-to-free-cash-flow line, which is flattered by
lease-and-capital intensity; on an earnings and enterprise basis this is a fairly-to-fully-priced
defensive.

On the economic moat: the durable edge is **scale-cost plus local density** — number-one/two

narrow-but-real moat, and it is **stable, not eroding** — returns on invested capital (~7.3%) and

having just reached online profitability — so the threat is **manageable**, not terminal. The
cheapness is best read as a modest fair-print on a steady compounder, not a structurally shrinking
base and not a deep bargain.

# Forensic Dossier — Ahold Delhaize (AD.AS)

*A deep dive on management and the setup, built from eight consecutive quarterly earnings calls (February 2025 through February 2026) cross-checked against the screener's hard financials.*

Ahold Delhaize is a pan-Atlantic grocery operator — it runs Albert Heijn and bol in the Netherlands, Delhaize in Belgium, Stop & Shop, Food Lion, Hannaford and Giant in the eastern United States, and Profi/Mega Image in Romania. It is a low-margin, high-volume, capital-intensive food retailer. The investment question is narrow: at roughly four times free cash flow, is the market pricing a structurally shrinking business, or is it simply ignoring a steady, cash-generative compounder?

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story has been remarkably consistent — almost monotonous — across all eight quarters, which for a defensive grocer is itself a positive signal. The spine is management's "Growing Together" strategy, unveiled in mid-2024 and repeated nearly verbatim every quarter since: grow sales faster than the industry at roughly a 4% compound annual rate, hold a leading underlying operating margin of about 4%, and convert that into steady earnings and free-cash-flow growth that funds dividends and buybacks.

What evolved within that frame is the emphasis. Early in 2025 the focus was on the heavy lifting — the Stop & Shop turnaround in the US (store closures, a $1 billion four-year price-investment program), the Belgium "Future Plan" franchise conversion, and integrating the Profi acquisition in Romania. By late 2025 and into the February 2026 call, the tone shifted toward harvesting: e-commerce reached full profitability "on a fully allocated basis" (a milestone management flagged as arriving earlier than expected), own-brand penetration climbed toward 39.8% group-wide (close to 50% in Europe), and retail media (advertising income) was repeatedly upgraded to a "growth machine."

Two growth drivers were introduced and amplified over time: retail media / advertising income, and artificial-intelligence-driven productivity (forecasting, store-first fulfillment, the Albert Heijn app, bol's "Spot & Shop"). Nothing material was quietly dropped — the Stop & Shop turnaround is still openly a multi-year project ("done in year four"), which is honest rather than evasive.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "~4% sales CAGR" (Growing Together) | Revenue €86.98B (2022) → €92.35B (2025); 3-yr CAGR +2.0%, latest year +3.4%; FY2025 net sales +5.9% (Profi/M&A-aided) | **Partly supported.** Organic comparable growth (~3.2% ex-gas in 2025) is real but the headline 4% leans on acquisitions and currency. |
| "~4% underlying operating margin, leading" | Reported underlying margin 4.0% in 2025; screener net margin 2.4%, gross 26.5% (stable) | **Supported.** The 4% is an *underlying operating* margin (pre-unusuals); the thin 2.4% net margin is normal for grocery and consistent. |
| "Strong free cash flow funding returns" | TTM free cash flow €5.27B; FY2025 FCF strong; 2026 guide ≥€2.3B; P/FCF ~4.2x | **Strongly supported** — and the crux of the value case. (Note the wide gap between the ~€5.3B TTM figure and the €2.3B forward guide; the guide is the conservative, post-capex run-rate to trust.) |
| EPS "mid-to-high single digit growth" | Diluted underlying EPS +7.8% in 2025; reported EPS €2.5 latest, +32% year-on-year off a depressed 2024 base; 5-yr EPS CAGR +3.6% | **Supported.** The +32% optical jump flatters a 2023–24 trough; the durable rate is the high-single-digit underlying figure. |
| "Online now profitable, fully allocated" | Margin stable, no separate disclosure | **Plausible but unverifiable from the financials** — management stopped breaking it out, which removes the ability to check it independently. |
| Stop & Shop "improving trends, gaining share" | US impairments ran ~€200M+/yr; management insists this is "incidental," not a run-rate | **Watch item.** The repeated US store impairments are the one place the narrative is richer than the evidence. |

The headline takeaway: the financials *corroborate* the cash-generation and margin claims, which are the load-bearing planks of a deep-value thesis. The growth claims are real but modest and partly bought. Returns are pedestrian — return on equity 14.6%, return on invested capital 7.3% — acceptable for capital-intensive grocery but not evidence of a widening moat.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Stable-to-rising, with disciplined restraint.** Management's confidence is steady and, if anything, firmer by the February 2026 call. Frans Muller (CEO) repeatedly bats away requests for segment-level or quarterly margin guidance — "live with the group guidance on margin, Rob" (May 2025) — which reads as discipline, not evasion, because the *group* guidance is specific and gets reiterated. The language stays offensive (growth, investment, densify-and-grow) rather than retreating into pure cost-defense, even while acknowledging a "volatile" macro backdrop (tariffs, egg prices, SNAP-benefit delays, Serbian price controls, Romanian VAT). CFO Jolanda Poots-Bijl is consistently the more conservative voice ("we take out pain rather early than later" on impairments), which lends credibility.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High.** The screener shows an earnings-beat rate of 6 of the last 7 quarters (86%). Across the transcript window management set group targets (≈4% growth, ≈4% margin, free cash flow floors) and then delivered against them — FY2025 landed at 4.0% underlying margin, +7.8% underlying EPS, and a reaffirmed dividend (+6% to €1.24) and €1 billion buyback. The Q1 2026 update reiterated full-year guidance (free cash flow of at least €2.3 billion, ~4% margin, mid-to-high-single-digit EPS growth) despite a seasonally negative Q1 free-cash-flow figure that management correctly pre-flagged as timing. There is a mild sandbagging pattern (the conservative €2.3B floor against ~€5.3B trailing). Reliability: **High.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts pushed hardest on three things, and management's handling tells you where the soft spots are:
- **US margin trajectory and Stop & Shop** — the most-asked topic, and the one management most consistently refuses to quantify quarter-by-quarter. The price-investment program ($1B over four years) is a margin headwind they ask the market to take on faith.
- **US store impairments** (UBS, August 2025) — a "EUR 200 million plus per year run rate" that management firmly disputes as incidental (Stop & Shop closures, Fresh Direct, fulfillment-center exits). If impairments persist beyond those one-offs, it would undercut the "store-first model is working" claim.
- **Profi (Romania)** — analysts flagged cut full-year sales guidance for Profi (November 2025), which management attributed to Romanian VAT and food-voucher timing, not structural weakness.

None of these has yet "turned into bad news," but the US price-investment margin drag is the live tension.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🟢 Reaffirmed and growing capital returns — €1B buyback plus a 40–50% payout dividend (+6% in 2025).
🟢 E-commerce reaching full-allocated profitability earlier than planned (February 2026) — removes a long-standing margin drag.
🟢 Consistent guidance delivery (86% beat rate) and a strong Piotroski financial-health score of 8/9.
🟢 Retail-media / advertising income emerging as a genuine high-margin growth lever.
🔴 Recurring US store impairments (~€200M/yr) that management insists are one-offs — needs to actually fade.
🔴 Online profitability de-disclosed ("we look at it holistically now") — convenient timing removes a check.
🔴 Returns are merely adequate (return on invested capital 7.3%) and the $1B US price-investment program is a self-imposed multi-year margin drag.
🟡 Growth is acquisition-assisted (Profi, Louis Delhaize), so organic momentum is slower than the headline.
